Lessons.Title: Distance Around Shapes
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM K–5 First Edition 2021 Grade 3 Unit 7 Lesson 6 teacher lesson, teacher preparation, student PDF (3 pages), all four blackline master shape pages, and the linked original illustration/vector references were read from the authorized machine. Publisher source visual graphics and paperclip photograph are linked, not embedded. The restricted original Cool-down remains unavailable. The source-to-first-party comparison does NOT claim source-material parity.

Lesson goals: perimeter is total boundary length of a flat two-dimensional shape. Not area, not the number of vertices or dots. Source times are Warm-up 10 min, Activity 1 15 min, Activity 2 20 min, synthesis 10 min, separately gated Cool-down 5 min. Source 3.MD.D.8; prerequisite count and add whole lengths, group equal lengths.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder: students observe an original photograph of paper clips placed end to end along one edge of a four-sided paper shape, then predict the number of equal-sized clips needed all the way around. Larger jumbo paper clips require FEWER clips than standard clips to cover the same boundary. There is no uniquely graded scalar answer; MLR8 discussion and teachers observe spatial reasoning.

Activity 1 original printed four separate blackline shapes, labelled A–D, are built with 1¼-inch paperclips in groups of four; each group uses about 25–50 paper clips. If using 1-inch paperclips, print the blackline masters at 80% scale. If the physical sizes or copying scale differ, the clip counts are not automatically transferable. Original teacher notes A uses 13 equal paperclips, B = 3×3 = 9, C = (2×4)+(2×2) = 12, and D = (2×6)+2 = 14, so D needs the MOST. Students should count along ALL sides; alternate repeated-addition and multiplication strategies are valid. Counting anchors are helpful but cannot substitute for constructing the shape, explaining the strategy and source measurements.

Activity 2 original source PDF page 3 includes FIVE labelled diagrams. A is a horizontal dot-grid rectangle 9 by 2 units (perimeter 22 grid units); B is a concave C-shaped eight-side dot-grid polygon (perimeter 26 grid units); C is a three-side triangle with boundary ticks (33 length intervals); D a four-side nonrectangular quadrilateral with ticks (32 intervals); E a six-sided shape with ticks (30 intervals). Original source SVG and corresponding PDF panels inspected for these five diagrams. The three latter tick-based diagrams use shared tick-interval counting for their comparison: C 33 > D 32 > E 30. The teacher expressly warns that the 22 in A and 33 in C are drawn with different physical unit lengths, so do NOT conclude C has a physically longer perimeter just because 33 is larger than 22.

A perimeter count must include each exterior or concave boundary segment ONCE. For dot grids count spaces between adjacent points, not the dots themselves. For marked sides count intervals between tick marks, including unmarked endpoints. On shape B do not overlook the four interior recess sides; 3+3+2+2+2+3+3+8=26. Comparing raw counts measured in different units is invalid unless the units are converted to a common length.

Learning representations: paper clips end-to-end; 2D exterior outline, grid/dot intervals, ticks on each side, addition of unequal sides, grouping repeated side lengths by multiplication. Teacher may accept any correctly justified construction/strategy. Oral explanation, hands-on paperclip construction, partner comparison, and unit consistency remain teacher-reviewed. Do not replace them with a single-number mastery claim.

Original lesson synthesis asks children to define perimeter and give practical uses such as picture frames, fencing or ribbon; both the context and original teacher questions are teacher-led. Separate Edulytics-authored numeric practice and Cool-down remain independent, NOT verbatim publisher Cool-down. Original publisher source graphics and paperclip images have NOT been added to the application; tests were written, not executed; Stage D/CI/academic sign-off remain deferred.

KeyConcepts.Title: Perimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Length along the entire boundary of a flat shape.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Sum every boundary segment in ONE common linear unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 9-by-2 rectangle has perimeter 2(9+2)=22 grid units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Paperclip unit
KeyConcepts.Definition: One equal-size paperclip can be used as a repeatable length unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Larger paperclip units mean fewer clips around the same shape.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original D needs 14 of the specified small clips; different-size clips require fresh measurement.

KeyConcepts.Title: Dot grid intervals
KeyConcepts.Definition: A unit is the distance between adjacent dots, not the dot count.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count intervals and concave recess edges.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original concave B has 26 dot-grid intervals around its outline.

KeyConcepts.Title: Side ticks
KeyConcepts.Definition: Marks partition each side into equal length intervals.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count intervals between marks and endpoints on all sides.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original C 33, D 32, E 30 ticks-as-length intervals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit-consistent comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Numeric measurements can be compared only in the same-sized length unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 22 dot units and 33 tick units cannot be compared as physical distances without a conversion.
KeyConcepts.Example: C 33 has largest among comparable tick-marked C, D, E; no justified comparison with A.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source paperclip prediction
WorkedExamples.Question: Which physical shape A–D requires most same-size source clips?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count every edge of each blackline shape.
Steps: A 13; B 9; C 12; D 14 of the specified paperclip unit.
Check that all clips are same size with no overlaps/gaps.
WorkedExamples.Check: Physically measuring or counting, teacher observation and correct printing scale required.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source concave dot-grid polygon
WorkedExamples.Question: What is the grid-unit perimeter of source figure B?
WorkedExamples.Method: Include all eight outer and inward boundary edges.
Steps: Top 3, upper right 3, first inset 2, inner vertical 2.
Second inset 2, lower right 3, bottom 3, left 8.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every boundary segment counted once; no dot-as-one-unit off-by-one.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source three tick-marked figures
WorkedExamples.Question: Which among C, D and E has the largest marked-interval perimeter?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count all intervals around comparable tick-marked sides.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not compare A 22 grid units with C 33 tick units without equal-length units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count dots/side tick marks instead of spaces.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Endpoint counting differs from the number of length units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count intervals BETWEEN adjacent dots or tick marks.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Skip the indentation on original shape B.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The cut-in edges are part of the boundary.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Trace every side continuously and once.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Compare source 22-grid rectangle to 33-tick triangle as if units match.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The lengths represented by those printed units are different.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare only measurements with equivalent units or convert them.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use 1-inch clips on original full-scale 1¼-inch blacklines without changing scale.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 13,9,12,14 source counts no longer correspond to original lengths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use specified clips, or scale page to 80%; teacher rechecks physical fit.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Interior tiles do not measure the boundary length.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Trace and sum only boundary segments.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up paperclip photo elicits talk, not a single numeric answer.
Blackline paperclip source A13, B9, C12, D14; D largest with specified scale and units.
Student source 6.2 A22, B26 grid units; C33, D32, E30 tick-interval units.
